unit.title: Forces
unit.blurb: Contact and non-contact forces, force diagrams and newtons, gravity, the difference between mass and weight, and air resistance.

O1.t: Identify contact and non-contact forces, draw force diagrams and measure forces in newtons.

O2.t: Describe gravity as an attraction that depends on mass and distance and keeps objects in orbit.

O3.t: Distinguish mass (kg) from weight (N) and explain why weight changes from place to place.

O4.t: Explain air resistance, why there is none in a vacuum, and how ideas about gravity developed.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 10: Forces.

When you ride a bicycle, forces are working all the time. You push the pedals, friction stops the wheels skidding, and the air pushes against you. Why do cyclists pedal harder into the wind? Let's find out about the forces around us.
A force is a push or a pull. You can push a trolley in front of you, or pull it along behind you.

Forces can make a still object start moving, or make a moving object stop. They can change an object's speed, its direction, or its shape. Forces always act in pairs, and always involve at least two objects.
Some forces only act when objects touch. These are contact forces. When a box rests on a floor, the floor pushes up on it with a normal force. When you push the box, you exert an applied force.
As the box slides, the floor exerts a frictional force. Friction opposes motion, acting against the applied force, and slows things down.
A stretched or squashed spring exerts a spring force. And a rope pulled tight from both ends has a tension force in it. If the pulls at each end are equal, nothing moves.
Other forces act at a distance, without touching. Gravitational force, or gravity, attracts objects towards each other. It's why an apple falls from a tree, and it gives objects their weight.
Electrical force acts between charged objects: opposite charges attract, and like charges repel. Magnetic force attracts some metals, and can push other magnets away.
So: normal, applied, friction, spring and tension forces are contact forces. Gravitational, electrical and magnetic forces act at a distance.
We show forces using a force diagram. On a windsurfer, the wind in the sail gives forward thrust, drag acts backwards, lift pushes up, and gravity pulls down.
Each arrow shows the direction of a force, and the length of the arrow shows its size. Force is measured in newtons, symbol N, named after the scientist Sir Isaac Newton.

We measure force with a force meter, also called a newton meter. Its spring stretches when a force is applied, moving a pointer along a scale. An apple with a mass of about 100 grams is pulled down by gravity with a force of about 1 newton.

q.prompt: Gravitational force gets weaker when objects…

captions: Gravity is a force of attraction between objects. It keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun, the Moon in orbit around the Earth, and keeps us on the ground. Why doesn't the Moon fall down? It's moving sideways, so as Earth pulls it in, Earth's surface curves away. The Moon keeps falling around the Earth, in an orbit!
The size of the gravitational force depends on mass. Objects with larger masses pull with a greater force, which is why we notice Earth's gravity so easily.
It also depends on distance. The further apart two objects are, the weaker the gravitational force between them. That's why astronauts far out in space feel almost weightless.

sections.title: Mass and weight

stops.note: Paused after: “So, mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms or grams, and it's th”

q.prompt: A 10 kg object on the Moon has a mass of…

captions: People often mix up mass and weight. Imagine an object with a mass of 10 kilograms. On Earth, gravity pulls on it with a force of about 98 newtons. That's its weight.
Take the same object to the Moon. It still contains the same amount of matter, so its mass is still 10 kilograms. But the Moon's gravity is weaker, so it weighs only about 16 newtons.
In outer space, far from any planet, there is almost no gravity, so its weight is about 0 newtons. But its mass is still 10 kilograms!

So, mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms or grams, and it's the same everywhere. Weight is the pull of gravity, measured in newtons, and it changes depending on where you are.

q.prompt: Who first described objects falling because of Earth's attraction?

captions: Cycling into a strong wind is hard work, because of air resistance, also called drag. It acts against an object moving through the air. When a skydiver jumps, gravity pulls him down, and air resistance pushes up. His surface area is small, so the drag is small and he falls fast.
When the parachute opens, its large surface area greatly increases the air resistance. The skydiver slows down and can land safely.
Racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars to reduce drag. Engineers test vehicles in wind tunnels: a vehicle with less drag needs less fuel, which is better for the environment.
Drop a ball and a feather from the same height. The ball lands first. The feather's shape and large surface area mean the air pushes against it much more, slowing it down.

Galileo found that objects of the same shape and size but different weights hit the ground together. In a vacuum, a space with no matter, not even air, there is no air resistance at all, so even a feather and a bowling ball fall at the same rate!
Outer space is almost a vacuum. Once a spacecraft leaves the atmosphere, there's no air resistance to slow it, so if it switches off its engine, it just keeps moving forward at the same speed.
Our ideas about gravity grew over many centuries. In India, the mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta was the first to describe objects falling because of Earth's force of attraction.
Later, Galileo Galilei experimented with falling objects and showed that objects of the same shape and size fall at the same rate, whatever their weight.

About a thousand years after Brahmagupta, in 1687, Isaac Newton published his Law of Universal Gravitation. He said that he could see further only by standing on the shoulders of giants: he built on the work of scientists before him.
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Name one force that acts only when objects touch, and one that acts at a distance. Pause the video now.
Answer: e.g. friction (contact); gravity or magnetism (at a distance).
Question 2: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon? Pause the video now.
Answer: Still 70 kg – mass doesn't change; only weight does.
Question 3: How does a parachute slow a skydiver down? Pause the video now.
Answer: Its large surface area increases air resistance.
Question 4: Why is there no air resistance in outer space? Pause the video now.
Answer: It is almost a vacuum – there is no air.
